references.text: Abraham travels to Egypt due to a famine, which mirrors how famines drive events in the lives of the patriarchs.
Isaac experiences a famine in the land, a parallel to repeated famines in the history of the patriarchs.
All nations came to Egypt to buy grain from Joseph, showing the worldwide scope of the famine described in verse 56.
Jacob's sons travel to Egypt to buy grain because of the famine—a direct result of the events in Genesis 41:56.
The famine was very severe, and Joseph collected all the silver in Egypt and Canaan by selling grain to the people.
God called a famine over the land and sent Joseph ahead—a poetic summary of the events in Genesis 41.
Stephen speaks about the famine that struck all of Egypt and Canaan, and how Jacob sent the fathers to Egypt—a direct reference to the story of Joseph.
Agabus prophesies about a great famine over the whole world, which mirrors the widespread famine in Joseph's time.
Describes the same sequence of events where the famine led the Egyptians to sell their land.
Confirms Joseph's role as ruler of the land and supplier of grain while introducing his brothers' encounter with him.
Emphasizes the total scope and intensity of the famine as the basis for Joseph's intervention.
Describes the economic consequence of the grain sales where money was collected for Pharaoh.
A New Testament allusion confirming the extent of the famine over both Egypt and Canaan as described in Genesis.
Describes the concrete handling of the grain sales as part of the general crisis.
Describes the brothers' direct response to the famine by traveling to Egypt for grain.
Creates a theological contrast by showing how Joseph's house was provided for while the rest of the country starved.
